transcript.content: Hi, welcome in — I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

I’ve been… hearing things. A man’s voice, mostly at work. It sounds like it’s coming through the garage vents, or sometimes from under the hood of a car. It’s clear—like he’s right there. He tells me not to trust my husband, or not to touch certain cars.
How long have you been hearing this man's voice — days, weeks, or longer?
Longer. Um… probably about ten months now. The voice, and feeling like I’m being tracked… it’s been going on most of this year.
During these past ten months, have you been using any alcohol, marijuana, stimulants, or other recreational drugs?
Um… not really. I mean, I’ll have a drink once in a while, but I’m not using drugs or anything like that.
During these past ten months, have you also gone through stretches where your mood was very low—or, on the other hand, unusually high or energetic—separate from what the voice is saying to you?

Yeah… I guess there are times I get really amped up. Like I feel like I could fix every car in the whole shop, like nobody can keep up with me. And then little stuff sets me off—my husband asking about dishes, or someone moving my socket set—I just… snap. It feels like they’re trying to hold me back.
When you're not feeling that amped-up, irritable energy—during times your mood feels more normal or even low—do you still hear that man's voice?

Yeah… it didn’t really stop. Even during a quieter few weeks, when I was sleeping more and not doing all these big plans, I still heard that voice at the garage. And I still felt like my husband and my boss were keeping tabs on me.

Thinking back over these full ten months, would you say the manic, high-energy or irritable stretches have taken up most of that time, or have there been long periods—weeks or months—where your mood was just steady and normal, even though you still heard the voice?
Most of it’s been those… wired stretches, I guess. Talking too fast, taking on too much at work, feeling like I can’t slow down. I don’t think there were many long normal times.
When you're in one of those amped-up, wired stretches, how long does it typically last before it settles down—days, or a week or more?
It’s not just a few days. It kind of… stretches on. I’d say it’s been going like that for months—close to the whole eleven months, really.

That quieter stretch you mentioned when you were sleeping more and not making big plans—how many weeks did that calmer period last, and during that whole time was your mood essentially normal, without feeling depressed or slowed down either?

It was just a few weeks, I think. I was sleeping more and not… doing all those big plans. I don’t know if I’d call it totally normal, but calmer, yeah. The voice at the garage was still there, though, and I still felt like my husband and my boss were tracking me.
Before these past ten months, had you ever heard that voice or felt like you were being tracked at any other time in your life, even when your mood was completely normal?

Before all this? I… I don’t really remember it like that. The main time I can point to was those quieter few weeks—when I was sleeping more and not making big plans—and even then the garage voice was still there. I still thought my husband and boss were tracking me.
During that calmer few-week stretch, did you notice any depressed mood, low energy, or hopelessness, or was your mood essentially neutral—neither high nor low—the whole time?

I don’t know… I was calmer, I guess. Sleeping more, not making all those big plans. But it wasn’t like everything was normal—the garage voice was still there, and I still thought my husband and my boss were tracking me.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a ~10-11 month history of persistent auditory hallucinations (a man's voice) and persecutory delusions (being tracked by husband/boss) that co-occur with a manic/irritable mood episode (grandiosity about fixing all cars, decreased need for sleep, irritability, rapid speech, increased goal-directed activity) lasting most of the illness course. Critically, during a brief calmer period when manic symptoms partially remitted, the hallucinations and delusions persisted, establishing that psychotic symptoms occur both during and independent of the mood episode. This concurrent presence of mood symptoms meeting manic criteria together with psychotic symptoms, plus psychotic symptoms persisting for a period without prominent mood symptoms, fits Schizoaffective Disorder, manic type (F25.0) rather than a primary mood disorder with psychotic features (where psychosis would be confined to mood episodes only) or schizophrenia (where mood symptoms would not be as prominent/concurrent). Substance use was denied, ruling out substance-induced psychosis.
